title: Specialist advice & the standards to follow
blurb: Know where to get specialist advice, which standards a project must adhere to, and the difference between what you must and should follow.
question: A project manager is delivering a new customer portal for an insurer. She must handle customers' personal data, meet a contract clause requiring an ISO 9001-certified quality approach, and manage risk consistently with the rest of the organisation. Where should she seek specialist advice, and which standards apply?

teach.h: Know the limits of your competence
teach.body: No project manager is an expert in everything. Part of being a professional is recognising when an issue is outside your competence and getting SPECIALIST ADVICE from an authoritative, accountable source. Alongside advice, projects must adhere to STANDARDS: the laws, regulations, professional codes, international standards and organisational policies that define how the work must, or should, be done. In plain English: ask the right expert, and follow the right rulebook.

teach.caption: HSE is the UK health and safety regulator; the ICO (Information Commissioner's Office) regulates data protection.

head: Question on the project
Ask
rows: How do we support a disabled colleague?
Is the site work plan safe?
How should we select a supplier?
Can we use customers' data this way?

head: Standard
Covers
rows: Recognised project terms and good practice
Ethical, professional behaviour of APM members
teach.caption: Plus industry regulations for your sector and your organisation's own policies and procedures.

teach.body: Not every standard carries the same weight. Laws and regulations are MANDATORY. Organisational policies are mandatory inside the organisation. International standards such as ISO 9001 are VOLUNTARY good practice, unless a contract, client or regulator requires them, at which point they become an obligation. The APM Body of Knowledge is good-practice guidance, while APM members are bound by the Code of Professional Conduct. Knowing which is which tells you what is negotiable and what is not.

teach.caption: A voluntary standard moves up the pyramid the moment a contract or regulator requires it.

teach.text: Classic traps. 1) ISO standards are NOT laws: they are voluntary unless a contract or regulator requires them. 2) Advice must be authoritative and accountable: forums, social media, friends and 'what we did last time' are not specialist sources. 3) Match the body to the topic: APM for project management, HSE for health and safety, ICO for data protection.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name specific sources: legal, HR, finance, health and safety, procurement, data protection officer.
Name standards: APM Body of Knowledge, Competence Framework, Code of Professional Conduct, relevant ISO standards.
Explain why: specialist accuracy, legal compliance, consistency, credibility, protecting people.
Distinguish mandatory (law, regulation, policy) from voluntary (ISO unless contracted).
Add how: seek advice early, use authoritative sources, record the advice and act on it.
Seek specialist advice when an issue is beyond your competence: legal, HR, finance, H&S, procurement, DPO.
External sources include regulators (HSE, ICO), professional bodies (APM) and specialist experts.
APM standards: Body of Knowledge, Competence Framework, Code of Professional Conduct.
ISO 21502 project management, ISO 9001 quality, ISO 14001 environmental, ISO 31000 risk.
Law and regulation are mandatory; ISO standards are voluntary unless a contract requires them.

summary: You can now name the main internal and external sources of specialist advice and match them to project questions. You can also list the standards a project manager may need to adhere to, and explain which are mandatory and which are good practice.

A.q: Which international standard gives guidance on project management?
A.why: ISO 21502 provides guidance on project management.

whyNot.2: ISO 31000 gives guidelines for risk management.

A.q: A project manager is unsure whether the project's planned use of customer data is lawful. Who is the most appropriate first source of advice inside the organisation?
A.why: The data protection officer advises on handling personal data lawfully under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

whyNot.0: Procurement advises on buying goods and services and managing suppliers.
whyNot.2: Finance advises on budgets and spending authority, not data protection law.
whyNot.3: The project office supports standards and reporting but isn't the data protection specialist.

A.q: Which APM publication sets out the ethical and professional behaviour expected of APM members?
A.why: The APM Code of Professional Conduct sets the ethical and professional standards APM members are expected to uphold.

whyNot.1: The Body of Knowledge sets out project management concepts, terms and good practice.
whyNot.2: The Competence Framework describes the competences of project professionals.
whyNot.3: A qualification handbook explains an exam and its syllabus.

B.q: Which statement about ISO standards such as ISO 9001 is correct?
options: They are UK laws that apply to all projects
They are voluntary unless a contract requires them
They apply only to public sector projects
B.why: ISO standards are voluntary good practice. They become obligations when a contract, client or regulator requires them.

whyNot.0: ISO standards are not laws; they are internationally agreed good practice.
whyNot.2: Organisational policies still apply; standards may shape them but don't replace them.
whyNot.3: ISO standards are used across the private and public sectors.

B.q: Which pairing of standard and subject is correct?
B.why: ISO 31000 provides guidelines for risk management.

whyNot.0: ISO 9001 is quality management; environmental management is ISO 14001.
whyNot.1: ISO 14001 is environmental management; quality management is ISO 9001.
whyNot.3: ISO 21502 is guidance on project management, not data protection.

B.q: Which is NOT a reliable source of specialist advice for a project manager?
B.why: Anonymous forums lack authority and accountability, so their advice can't be relied on for project decisions.

whyNot.0: The legal team is an authoritative internal source of legal advice.
whyNot.1: HSE is the UK regulator for health and safety and publishes authoritative guidance.
whyNot.3: The APM Body of Knowledge is a recognised source of project management good practice.

C.q: On a construction project, site supervisors disagree about how often scaffolding must be inspected. What should the project manager do?
options: Use the interval the most senior foreman likes
Seek advice from the H&S adviser and guidance
Ask the team to vote and record the outcome
Choose the longest interval to save schedule
C.why: This is a specialist safety question. The health and safety adviser, using official requirements and HSE guidance, gives an authoritative answer.

whyNot.0: Seniority is not a substitute for specialist, authoritative advice.
whyNot.2: Safety requirements are not decided by a vote.
whyNot.3: Putting schedule ahead of safety ignores legal duties and risks harm.

C.q: An iterative team is building an app that processes personal data. What is the best way to make data protection advice part of delivery?
options: Ask the DPO to review the app after launch
Leave it to the supplier's own developers
Treat data protection as a 'Could have'
Involve the DPO early, in the definition of done
C.why: Bringing the data protection officer in early and building data protection checks into the definition of done means every increment meets the requirements.

whyNot.0: Reviewing after launch is too late; non-compliant processing may already have happened.
whyNot.1: The organisation stays responsible; it can't simply hand compliance to developers.
whyNot.2: Legal requirements are not optional, so they can't be a 'Could have'.

C.q:
Which THREE are standards or rules a project manager may need to adhere to?
1. APM Code of Professional Conduct
2. Organisational policies
3. ISO 9001, where the contract requires it
4. A supplier's sales brochure
C.why: The APM code (for members), organisational policies and contractually required ISO standards are all standards to adhere to.

whyNot.1: A sales brochure (4) is marketing, not a standard.
whyNot.2: Includes the sales brochure (4) and leaves out organisational policies (2).
whyNot.3: Includes the sales brochure (4) and leaves out the APM code (1).

reteach.title: Building a house extension
reteach.question: You're planning a kitchen extension. Your builder is great at building, but who do you ask about the steel beam, the boundary wall and the drains, and which rules must you follow?

blocks.body: A good builder knows when to say 'that's a question for the structural engineer'. The engineer sizes the beam, a party wall surveyor handles the shared wall, and building control checks the work meets the Building Regulations, which are law. Product standards are good practice unless your contract with the builder says they must be met. Asking a neighbour or an online forum instead would be cheaper, and risky.

head: Question
Expert
rows: How big must the beam be?

blocks.text: The builder (like a project manager) doesn't have to know everything, but they must know when to ask and who to ask.

explain.body: Most organisations have specialist functions to call on: legal, HR, finance, health and safety, procurement and a data protection officer. Use them whenever a question is outside your own competence.

test.q: A team member asks for adjustments to their working pattern because of a long-term health condition. Which internal function should the project manager consult?
test.why: HR specialists advise on employment matters, including reasonable adjustments and working patterns.

whyNot.0: Procurement deals with buying from suppliers.
whyNot.1: Finance deals with budgets and spending.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports project standards and reporting, not employment advice.

explain.body: Regulators publish authoritative guidance: HSE for health and safety, the ICO for data protection. Professional bodies such as APM set professional standards. Specialist experts, such as a chartered engineer, advise on technical matters.

test.q: A project team needs authoritative UK guidance on meeting its data protection obligations. Where should it look?
test.why: The Information Commissioner's Office is the UK regulator for data protection and publishes guidance on UK GDPR.

whyNot.0: HSE regulates health and safety, not data protection.
whyNot.2: A supplier's marketing team isn't an authoritative or independent source.
whyNot.3: A podcast may be interesting but isn't an authoritative regulatory source.

explain.body: APM: Body of Knowledge, Competence Framework, Code of Professional Conduct. International: ISO 21502 (project management guidance), ISO 9001 (quality), ISO 14001 (environmental), ISO 31000 (risk). Plus industry regulations and organisational policies.

test.q: A client asks for evidence that the project's environmental management follows a recognised international standard. Which is most relevant?
test.why: ISO 14001 is the international standard for environmental management systems.

explain.body: Seek advice early, from authoritative and accountable sources. Brief the specialist clearly, record the advice and its source, and act on it. If two sources conflict, check with the most authoritative, current one.

test.q: A project manager receives conflicting advice on a regulatory point from a colleague and from a trade magazine. What should she do?
options: Merge the two into one approach
test.why: Conflicting advice should be resolved by going to the most authoritative, current source, such as the regulator's guidance or the relevant specialist.

whyNot.0: Blending two possibly wrong answers doesn't make a right one.
whyNot.1: Cost doesn't make advice correct or compliant.
whyNot.2: The order advice arrives in says nothing about its accuracy.
